newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Latest Caspian row should not deter new oil deals.
newsitem.headline: Latest Caspian row should not deter new oil deals.

text.p: A decision by Russia's state oil company Rosneft to pull out of a deal to develop a disputed Caspian oilfield was an isolated case and should in no way derail the great Caspian oil game, energy analysts said Friday.

But the row between Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan over who owns the deposit, straddling the border between Turkmen and Azeri territory, highlights the need for a permanent solution between littoral states over who owns the rights to what.
"The areas of dispute are limited. This is neither a trend nor a significant precedent," said Manouchehr Takin, senior analyst at the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London.

The latest chapter in the long debate over the Caspian's status flared up after Rosneft signed a preliminary deal with Russia's largest oil company LUKoil and Azerbaijan's state oil firm SOCAR to jointly develop the field.

Under the $1 billion deal SOCAR was to get a 50 percent share, LUKoil 30 percent and Rosneft 20 percent. The field, known as Kyapaz by Azerbaijan and as Serdar by Turkmenistan, is estimated to contain over 50 million tonnes of recoverable oil.

LUKoil said it would stay in the deal, but could not confirm whether it would bid for Rosneft's share or if a third party would be chosen. It said disputes over the status of the Caspian would not dampen its interest in the resource-rich region.
"LUKoil is not going to wait for politicians to untangle themselves," LUKoil spokesman Pyotr Neyev said. "We need to work. We have a guarantee from the Azeri government, and that is enough for us."

Rosneft was also careful not to isolate itself from one of the most promising energy sources in the world. Spokesman Vladimir Vyunitsky said Rosneft president Yuri Bespalov planned to visit the Azeri capital Baku and Turkmenistan's capital Ashgabat to discuss other deals in the region.
Analysts said it was rare for a company to pull out of a deal because of territorial disputes, but that it would be business as usual once the dust over Kyapaz/Serdar settled.

"Deals will go on being made in isolation," said Stewart Johnston, upstream director at Arthur D. Little consultants in London. "There will be hiccups like this one, but it's not going to cause a wider stir."

With hundreds of millions of tonnes of black gold lying under the Central Asian water body, not to mention huge reserves of gas, the stakes are high. So far Azerbaijan leads the way in attracting foreign firms to jointly develop offshore reserves.

But the five countries bordering the Caspian are still at loggerheads on how to carve up the territory, a dispute which some energy executives have said is slowing development of oil and gas deposits in the region.
Russia and Iran treat the Caspian as a huge lake, and argue that energy reserves should be developed jointly by all sides.
Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan say it is a sea, and should be split into separate territories.
The picture has been further muddied by the spat between Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan over some fields which straddle territorial divisions.
A third factor is Russia's apparently contradictory position. One the one hand it says its official definition of the Caspian as a lake still holds.
But in the same breath it appears to be promoting Russian companies in the Caspian as a way of keeping some presence in a region it used to dominate during Soviet times.
Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov is due in Moscow on September 7 to meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin, and the status of the Caspian is likely to be high on the agenda.

Azerbaijan says it is willing to discuss disputed fields with Turkmenistan. But it is unlikely to want to bring up for discussion two big fields already being developed by a major international consortium that includes SOCAR.
Turkmenistan says the fields, called Chirag and Azeri by Azerbaijan, belong partially to Turkmenistan in the first case and fully in the second.
The Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC), an $8-billion consortium led by British Petroleum and Norway's Statoil and including SOCAR, says it is unfazed by the spat.
It plans to start producing shortly, and says reserves in the contract area containing the two fields are 550 million tonnes of oil and 82 billion cubic feet of gas.

Analysts do not exclude the possibility that Rosneft's withdrawal from the "Kyapaz" deal is tied to internal fighting between president Yuri Bespalov and board chairman Alexander Putilov, who have opposing views on the company's future.
Putilov signed the original deal during Azeri president Haydar Aliyev's visit to Moscow last month, but was not part of the decision to annul it on Thursday. Bespalov, however, was.
The squabble has intensified in recent weeks as the sale of 51 percent of the company approaches.
